lessons.title: Financial analysis with ratios
lessons.html:
Analysing financial statements

At N6 level the manager uses the income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement to assess the financial health of the farm business and to communicate with lenders and investors. Ratios make figures comparable between years and between farms.

Example figures (R thousand)

ItemValue
Current assets1,800
Current liabilities1,200
Total assets24,000
Total liabilities7,200
Net farm income (after interest)1,050
Interest paid690
Gross farm income9,600

Liquidity

Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities = 1,800 / 1,200 = 1.5. This measures the ability to meet short-term obligations. A ratio below 1 indicates possible difficulty in paying debts due within the year.

Solvency

Debt ratio = total liabilities / total assets = 7,200 / 24,000 = 0.30 (30%). The owner's equity ratio is therefore 70%. Higher debt ratios increase financial risk, especially when interest rates rise or a drought cuts income.

Profitability

Return on total assets = (net farm income + interest) / total assets = (1,050 + 690) / 24,000 = 7.25%. Adding interest back measures how well all assets perform regardless of how they are financed. A return on assets below the cost of borrowing means debt is reducing the owner's return. Some analysts also deduct a management allowance first; use a consistent method.

Return on equity = net farm income / owner's equity = 1,050 / 16,800 = 6.25%.

Efficiency

Interest expense ratio = interest / gross farm income = 690 / 9,600 = 7.2%. Asset turnover = gross farm income / total assets = 0.40. Land-intensive farming typically has a low asset turnover, so small improvements in margin matter.

Interpreting ratios

Always interpret ratios as trends over several years and against benchmarks for similar enterprises and regions. Note that land valuations strongly affect solvency and return ratios; state whether market or historical values are used.

lessons.title: Investment appraisal, financing and risk
lessons.html:
Capital investment decisions

Investments in land, orchards, irrigation, solar power, dairies or machinery commit large sums for many years. Appraisal methods help rank alternatives.

Payback period

The time taken for net cash inflows to repay the investment. A R600,000 solar installation saving R150,000 per year in electricity has a payback of 4 years. Payback is simple and highlights liquidity risk, but ignores cash flows after payback and the time value of money.

Time value of money

A rand received in future is worth less than a rand today because money today can earn interest. Discounting converts future cash flows to present values: PV = future amount / (1 + r) raised to the power n, where r is the discount rate and n the number of years. At 10%, R150,000 received in year 3 is worth about R112,700 today.

Net present value and internal rate of return

  • NPV = sum of discounted net cash flows minus initial investment. A positive NPV means the investment earns more than the required rate of return.
  • IRR is the discount rate at which NPV equals zero. Compare it with the cost of capital.

For long-term crops such as macadamias or citrus, the negative cash flows during establishment and the years to full bearing make discounting essential. Include residual values, replacement costs and realistic yield build-up.

Financing the farm

NeedTypical source
Seasonal inputsProduction credit, overdraft, co-op or input-supplier credit
Machinery and vehiclesInstalment sale or lease
Land and long-term developmentMortgage bond from commercial banks or the Land Bank
ExpansionOwner's equity, partners, development finance

Match the term of finance to the life of the asset: do not finance an orchard with an overdraft. Lenders assess repayment capacity from cash flow budgets, security, the owner's equity and management track record.

Financial risk management

  • Maintain cash reserves and unused credit capacity.
  • Use crop and asset insurance.
  • Hedge prices with forward contracts or futures and options on the JSE commodity derivatives market where appropriate.
  • Stress-test cash flow and debt servicing at higher interest rates and lower yields and prices.

Key points

  • Use liquidity, solvency, profitability and efficiency ratios, interpreted as trends and against benchmarks.
  • Return on assets below the cost of borrowing means debt reduces the owner's return.
  • Payback is simple; NPV and IRR account for the time value of money.
  • Match the term of finance to the life of the asset.
  • Manage financial risk with reserves, insurance, hedging and stress tests.
